newsitem.title: USA: U.S. tobacco to seek delay in Mississippi trial.
newsitem.headline: U.S. tobacco to seek delay in Mississippi trial.

text.p: Lawyers for the U.S. tobacco industry said Wednesday they would ask a Mississippi judge to delay until September the trial of the state's landmark case against cigarette makers.

Mississippi Attorney General Mike Moore vowed to fight any change in the scheduled June 2 start of the trial, in Jackson County Chancery Court. He also said he would ask the judge to begin reviewing Liggett Group documents for possible inclusion in the proceedings.
The two sides were scheduled to appear before Judge William Myers at a hearing set for 1400 EST/1900 GMT.

"There's no way this case can be ready to go to trial (in June)," said Joe Colingo, a local lawyer representing the tobacco industry. "If it does, it will be the biggest injustice that has been perpetrated by the court system."

Mississippi is one of 22 states seeking to recoup Medicaid funds spent treating poor people for smoking-related illnesses in recent decades. All told, the states are trying to get back an estimated $30 billion in expenditures.
Moore, the first state attorney general to file suit against the tobacco industry, hopes Mississippi's suit alone will recoup nearly $1 billion.
Brooke Group Ltd's Liggett handed over internal documents last month as part of a settlement with 22 state attorneys general.

Mississippi officials believe the documents, which have largely remained sealed, will support their claim that industry executives knew about the hazards of smoking decades ago but altered their own research to conceal the truth.

Last week, the judge in a $650 million second-hand-smoke suit brought by the family of a Mississippi barber who died from cancer in 1994 ruled that 11 Liggett documents could be turned over to plaintiffs in that case.
The tobacco industry appealed the order to the Mississippi Supreme Court, which issued a stay of the order until April 11 so that justices would have time to review the case.
"Whatever the Supreme Court said would apply in that case would equally apply in this case," Colingo said, adding that he would oppose any discussion about the Liggett issue at today's hearing.
The tobacco industry says the trial date must be delayed because 61 potential witnesses, including 34 experts and 17 Medicaid recipients, have not yet been deposed by lawyers.
Colingo blamed Mississippi state officials, saying they had refused to hand over information to defendants. "They're stonewalling," he said.
The state contends that most of the potential witnesses have already been deposed.
Moore said cigarette makers have asked for similar delays in suits in Florida, Texas, Minnesota and Washington.
"The point we're going to make today is that this is not just playing out in Mississippi," he said.
